case_study_insert.main_stem: VoltLine Mobility (VLM) is a private limited company in the electric mobility and digital platform sector, employing a workforce of 42. Founded in 2017 by Sofia Marchetti, who also chairs the board, the business operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. VLM plans to invest $720,000 in an automated e-bike battery-swapping network with contactless payment kiosks, financed by a $450,000 eight-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $330,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $33, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. VLM faces an operational problem: complaints about scooter condition are rising and the defect rate on returned scooters has reached 2.7%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: VLM recorded 9,600 rides with a 97.4% on-time battery-swap rate, down from 98.9% a year earlier. Complaints about scooter condition rose from 31 to 58 per month, and average swap time is 3.4 minutes. A survey of 700 riders found 63% prefer contactless payment and 49% would pay $1.50 more for guaranteed battery availability. Manual inspection of a returned scooter takes 12 minutes per unit.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of VoltLine Mobility for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.90 to $14.71 per hour from January 2027. (3) Lithium battery input costs have risen 14.2% year-on-year, and consumer spending on mobility services grew 4.8% in the same period.

questions.question_text: VLM is financing part of its battery-swapping expansion with an eight-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for VLM of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit has no interest or repayment obligation, so VLM preserves the cash that would service the $450,000 eight-year bank loan. That cash can be spent on the $720,000 automated swapping network and on fixing the 2.7% defect rate on returned scooters without increasing the $330,000 annual fixed costs or the $33 selling price.

Point 2: Funding with $270,000 retained profit leaves Sofia Marchetti and the board free of lender conditions on how the contactless payment kiosks are rolled out, which matters when 58 riders a month already complain about scooter condition. It also avoids risking company assets if the 97.4% on-time swap rate cannot be restored, giving VLM time to improve service before adding debt. Given that 49% of riders would pay $1.50 more for guaranteed battery availability, internally funded investment can improve the service that generates that revenue, while interest on the $450,000 loan would absorb cash needed to answer the 58 monthly complaints.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to VLM and its expansion financing.

questions.question_text: VLM is launching its new battery-swapping network. Consider local radio sponsorship, outdoor poster advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should VLM choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio sponsorship: Radio is affordable and can reach commuters in the cities where the 9,600 rides are taken, with quick turnaround for launch messages. Its limit is that it cannot show the contactless kiosks or explain battery availability, and sound alone does not reach the 700 riders surveyed who compare services online.

Outdoor poster advertising: Posters near transport hubs can build high visibility for the $720,000 network and repeatedly reach the people most likely to ride. However, production and site costs are high, the message cannot be changed quickly if the 97.4% on-time swap rate is criticised, and reach is confined to the poster locations.

Social media influencer marketing: Mobility reviewers can demonstrate the kiosks and the swapping process to a large online audience at low cost per view, with measurable engagement. This connects with the 63% of riders who prefer contactless payment and the 49% who would pay $1.50 more for guaranteed battery availability, while allowing VLM to answer the 58 monthly complaints publicly and show improvements.

Recommendation: VLM should choose social media influencer marketing. It demonstrates the product, targets riders online and is far cheaper than posters. Radio is rejected because it cannot show a visual service and is limited geographically; posters are rejected as costly and inflexible for a firm servicing a $450,000 loan. Influencer content should be paired with in-app notifications to existing riders. The 3.4-minute swap time and 58 complaints mean the campaign should show real improvements, which influencer video can do; posters and radio cannot demonstrate a working kiosk or answer rider concerns.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to VLM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of VLM with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and posters are rejected.

questions.question_text: VLM faces rising complaints about scooter condition and a 2.7% defect rate. Explain two benefits for VLM of using democratic leadership within its hierarchical structure to improve motivation among its 42 staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 42 employees to suggest how scooters are checked before each swap, so the people handling the machines can help reduce the 2.7% defect rate. Involvement raises commitment and makes staff more careful, directly addressing the rise from 31 to 58 complaints a month and protecting the 9,600 rides recorded last quarter.

Point 2: The hierarchical structure keeps clear responsibility for the 3.4-minute swap time, so suggestions can be routed to the right supervisor and acted on without confusion. Staff who are consulted about the $720,000 swapping network are more likely to support the change, which helps Sofia Marchetti restore the 97.4% on-time battery-swap rate while keeping the $450,000 loan serviceable. Since the 97.4% on-time rate has fallen from 98.9%, employee ideas about maintenance are the most direct way to recover it; democratic consultation makes the 42 staff responsible for the 9,600 rides part of the solution.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VLM's complaints, defect rate and swap performance.

questions.question_text: VLM wants to cut complaints about scooter condition. Consider more frequent manual inspection, which takes 12 minutes per scooter, or an automated battery-monitoring and computer stock-control system. Which should VLM choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
More frequent manual inspection: Extra checks by staff can catch the faults behind the 2.7% defect rate and the 58 monthly complaints before riders see them, and it needs no new technology. The drawback is the time: at 12 minutes per scooter, more inspection across 9,600 rides would consume a great deal of the 42 workers' time, slowing the 3.4-minute swap service and raising costs while the $450,000 loan must be serviced.

Automated battery-monitoring and computer stock control: Sensors and software flag failing batteries automatically and track spare stock, preventing faults before a rider collects a scooter and supporting the $720,000 network. This suits VLM's automated strategy and can protect the 97.4% on-time swap rate. The insert gives no purchase price for such a system, so no defensible cost figure can be invented; the judgement rests on time saved against the 12-minute manual check.

Decision: VLM should choose the automated battery-monitoring and computer stock-control system. It addresses the cause of the 58 complaints, saves the 12 minutes per scooter that manual checks consume and fits the technology platform. More manual inspection is rejected as slow and labour-heavy for 9,600 rides, though a light manual check should remain as a final safety backstop. The monitoring system should be introduced at the busiest kiosks first, where 9,600 rides create the most pressure, and its effect measured against the 2.7% defect rate and 58 complaints. Because no purchase price is stated, the decision compares the 12 minutes of manual work per scooter with the time saved, not with an invented cost. A small manual check can remain for safety, so the choice is not between technology and no checks but between labour-heavy and automated detection.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two inspection approaches with limited application to VLM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both approaches in the context of VLM.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches with a well-justified decision covering time, defect rate, cost and service quality.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VLM's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $330,000 ÷ ($33 − $9) = $330,000 ÷ $24 = 13,750 units. Answer: break-even output is 13,750 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $33 − $9 = $24. Answer: contribution per unit is $24.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VLM's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 13,750-unit break-even output with 40,000 units produced, giving a margin of safety of 26,250 rides, so management can see how far demand could fall before the $720,000 network stops covering costs.
2. Use the $24 contribution per unit to test pricing: a $2 cut to $31 leaves $22 contribution, so about 15,000 rides (330,000 ÷ 22) would then be needed to cover the $330,000 fixed costs.
3. Average total cost is $17.25 a unit ($330,000 ÷ 40,000 = $8.25 plus $9), below the $33 price, leaving scope to absorb a higher battery cost.
4. Labour productivity is about 952 rides per worker (40,000 ÷ 42), a benchmark for judging whether automated monitoring improves output per employee.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 13,750 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $24 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 26,250 rides; a $2 price cut leaving $22 contribution and about 15,000 rides needed; average total cost of $17.25 against $33; labour productivity of about 952 rides per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VLM's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin and the profit margin for 2024 and 2025. Has VLM's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 44.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 48.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 24.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 30.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 revenue 1,250, cost of sales 700, gross profit 550; operating profit 300; capital employed 2,000. 2025 revenue 1,500, cost of sales 780, gross profit 720; operating profit 450; capital employed 2,250. Gross profit ÷ revenue: 550 ÷ 1,250 and 720 ÷ 1,500. Operating profit ÷ revenue: 300 ÷ 1,250 and 450 ÷ 1,500. Operating profit ÷ capital employed: 300 ÷ 2,000 and 450 ÷ 2,250.

Evaluation: All the measures improved. The share of revenue left after direct costs rose from 44.0% to 48.0% because revenue grew by 250 while cost of sales grew by only 80, showing the platform is scaling efficiently across 40,000 rides. The share kept as operating profit also rose, and the return on the 2,250 of capital employed improved, which matters because VLM must service a $450,000 loan while spending $720,000 on the swapping network. The 2.7% defect rate and 58 monthly complaints remain a risk, but they have not yet prevented stronger profits.

Conclusion: VLM's financial position has improved. Both margins and the return on capital are higher, driven by revenue growth faster than cost of sales rather than by cutting service quality. Management should reinvest part of the gain in the automated monitoring system so that the 97.4% on-time rate is protected and the improvement continues. Interest payable of 50 in 2025 remains small beside operating profit of 450, so financing costs are not driving the result.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the two margins for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost, profit and capital trends, and a justified conclusion on whether VLM improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VLM of introducing contactless payment kiosks across its battery-swapping network.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 700 riders found 63% prefer contactless payment and 49% would pay $1.50 more for guaranteed battery availability, so kiosks can raise revenue per ride and speed up the 3.4-minute swap process. The extra contribution helps cover $330,000 of fixed costs and supports the $720,000 network without pushing the $33 price higher.

Disadvantage: Installing and maintaining kiosks adds to the $330,000 fixed costs or the $9 variable cost per unit, and any payment failure would add to the 58 monthly complaints at a time when the 97.4% on-time rate is already under pressure. The insert gives no kiosk cost, so the exact return cannot be calculated from the data supplied. The kiosks should be introduced alongside the $1.50 guarantee that 49% of riders accept, but the 97.4% on-time rate must be restored first; otherwise a fast payment system would simply expose the underlying service problem to more riders.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VLM's survey, swap time and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase to $14.71 and the 14.2% rise in lithium battery input costs will affect VLM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If the $450,000 eight-year bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.75% × $450,000 = $3,375 a year, shown as 0.0075 × $450,000. This is small relative to $330,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed the direct effect is zero. The indirect risk is that higher rates dampen consumer spending on mobility services, which grew only 4.8%.

Minimum wage increase (5.8% to $14.71 an hour): No hours worked or existing pay are given, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented. The derivable measure is productivity: 40,000 units ÷ 42 workers = about 952 rides per worker. If that holds, the wage rise is absorbed through output; if the 2.7% defect rate and 58 complaints slow swaps, unit labour costs rise and the $24 contribution is squeezed. The effect cannot be quantified further from the insert.

Battery input-cost inflation (14.2%): The insert does not break down the $9 variable cost, so an explicit upper bound is 14.2% × $9 = $1.278, about $1.28 per ride. At 40,000 rides that is 40,000 × $1.28 = $51,200 a year. Even a partial pass-through cuts contribution from $24 toward $22.72, raising the break-even volume well above 13,750 rides.

Conclusion: The 14.2% rise in lithium battery costs will have the greatest impact. It hits every one of the 40,000 rides and directly erodes the $24 contribution that must cover $330,000 fixed costs and service the $450,000 loan, whereas the interest rise is about $3,375 and the wage effect is smaller and uncertain. VLM can recover part of the rise through the $1.50 premium that 49% of riders accept.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to VLM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VLM's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown derivations from insert figures and a well-justified greatest-impact judgement.
